title: Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā

atts.t:
One who does not apprehend the supreme perfection of wisdom,
Does not apprehend the bodhisattva, and does not apprehend the mind of awakening—
Upon hearing this, the one who is without bewilderment and without fear,
That bodhisattva practices the wisdom of the Sugatas.

i.sp: One who does not apprehend the supreme perfection of wisdom, / Does not apprehend the bodhisattva, and does not apprehend the mind of awakening— / Upon hearing this, the one who is without bewilderment
i.ev: Tibetan 'གང་ལ་ ... མི་དམིགས་ཤིང་། ... མི་དམིགས། ... མི་དམིགས། དེ་སྐད་ཐོས་ནས་' is a locative construction (Sanskrit 'yasmin ... na ... upalabdhi'): in that case the perfection of wisdom, the bodhisattva and the mind of awakening are not apprehended; the three are passive objects, not things 'one' fails to apprehend. Mipham 1-4 glosses 'བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ལ་ ... ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་མཆོག་ ... མི་དམིགས་', and 'དེ་སྐད་ཐོས་ནས' is hearing that teaching of non-apprehension. The English subject ('One who ...') is stacked with a second 'the one who' and the demonstrative 'this' has no clear antecedent, so it is hard to see what is heard.
i.fx: In whom the supreme perfection of wisdom is not apprehended, nor the bodhisattva, nor the mind of awakening—having heard such [teaching], without bewilderment and without fear, that bodhisattva practices the wisdom of the Sugatas.

atts.t:
In whom the supreme perfection of wisdom is not apprehended,
And the bodhisattva is not apprehended, nor the mind of awakening—
Having heard this, without bewilderment and without fear,
That bodhisattva practices the wisdom of the Sugatas.

judge.reason: B correctly uses the passive construction "In whom... is not apprehended," directly matching the locative "gang la" and the Sanskrit "yasmin."

i.sp: In them, there is not even an atom of a dwelling place for consciousness. / They do not dwell on any phenomena
i.ev: In lines 3-4 the Tibetan subject 'དེ' (Sanskrit 'sa', 'tasya' in line 2) is the single bodhisattva who practises ('དེ་ཆོས་ཀུན་ལ་མི་གནས་ ... བྱང་ཆུབ་འཐོབ'). Rangjung 1-5 makes this explicit: 'བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དེ་ལ། རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་བདེན་པའི་གནས་ནི་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་ཙམ་ཡང་ཡོད་པ་མ་ཡིན'. In the English, 'them' in line 2 refers back to form, feeling, perception and volition, so 'They' in lines 3-4 can be read as those four aggregates, and the bodhisattva is never named.
i.fx: For that one there is not even an atom of a dwelling place for consciousness. That one does not dwell on any phenomena but practices without a dwelling place; without grasping, that one attains the awakening of the Sugatas.

judge.reason: A's "For that one" and "That one" correctly and unambiguously reflect the singular referent (the bodhisattva), whereas B's "them"/"They" risks confusion with the aggregates.

atts.t:
Furthermore, examining, "What is this wisdom, and whose is it?
From where does it come?", they understand all these phenomena as empty;
Having closely examined them, without discouragement or fear—
That bodhisattva is close to awakening.

i.sp: they understand all these phenomena as empty
i.ev: Tibetan 'ཆོས་འདི་ཐམས་ཅད་སྟོང་པར་རྟོག' has 'རྟོག' (consider, examine), not 'རྟོགས' (realize); Sanskrit 'vyuparīkṣate ... śūnyaka sarva dharmāḥ' is 'examines'. Mipham 1-7: 'ཆོས་འདི་ཐམས་ཅད་རང་གི་ངོ་བོས་སྟོང་པར་རྟོག་ཅིང་དཔྱད་པར་བྱེད་དོ' (contemplates and investigates as empty); Khenrab 1-7 the same. The English claims realized understanding, and also renders 'རྟོག' as 'conceptualize' in 1-8, so the same word is treated inconsistently.
i.fx: they consider all these phenomena to be empty

atts.t:
Furthermore, examining, "What is this wisdom, and whose is it?
From where does it come?" they consider all these phenomena to be empty;
Having closely examined them, without discouragement or fear—
That bodhisattva is close to awakening.

judge.reason: B accurately translates "rtog" as "consider" (which fits the context of examining/investigating), whereas A's "understand" is too definitive.

atts.t:
Whatever bodhisattva abides here thus in peace
Has received the prophecy from the Tathāgatas of the past;
They have no conceit, thinking, "I am in meditative equipoise," or "I have arisen."
Why is this? Because they completely understand the nature of phenomena.

i.sp: abides here thus in peace
i.ev: Tibetan 'འདིར་བདག་ཞིར་གནས་པ' (Sanskrit 'evātmaśānti viharan') has 'བདག' (oneself): one abides at peace within oneself. Mipham 1-10: 'བདག་གི་རྒྱུད་ཉེ་བར་ཞིར་གནས་པ' (one's own mindstream abides at peace); Khenrab 1-10: 'བདག་གི་རྒྱུད་ ... ཉེ་བར་ཞི་བ'. The English drops 'བདག'.
i.fx: abides here thus, at peace within themselves

atts.t:
Whatever bodhisattva abides here thus, at peace within themselves,
Has received the prophecy from the Tathāgatas of the past;
They have no conceit, thinking, "I am in meditative equipoise," or "I have arisen."
Why is this? Because they completely understand the nature of phenomena.

i.sp: "I have arisen."
i.ev: Tibetan "བདག་ནི་མཉམ་པར་བཞག་ཅེའམ་ལངས་" (Skt vyutthita): "ལངས" means rising up out of equipoise; bo-mipham 1-10 glosses it "དེ་ལས་ལངས་སོ" (I have risen from it). "I have arisen" can be read as "I have come into being".
i.fx: "I am in meditative equipoise," or "I have risen from it."

judge.reason: A successfully translates "bdag" (self/ātma) as "within themselves," whereas B drops it entirely.

i.sp: the illusions of Māra
i.ev: Tibetan བདུད་ཀྱི་སྒྱུ་འདུལ་བ; Sanskrit namuciṃ śaṭha (deceitful Māra). Mipham (bo-mipham 1-17) glosses བདུད་ཀྱི་སྒྱུ་རྩལ, i.e. Māra's tricks/wiles, not "illusions" (which suggests magical appearance, སྒྱུ་མ).
i.fx: the wiles of Māra

i.sp: they subdue ... they are proclaimed to be a great being
i.ev: Plural "they/They" is followed by the singular "a great being"; the Tibetan སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེ is the single predicate of one bodhisattva.
i.fx: they are proclaimed to be great beings

judge.reason: A correctly uses the singular title "a great being" to correspond with the singular "mahasattva," whereas B switches to the plural "great beings."

atts.t:
For example, just as a magician conjures an emanation at a crossroads,
And cuts off the tens of millions of heads of a large crowd of people—
Whatever those to be killed are like, just so the bodhisattva
Fully knows all wanderers to be like emanations, and has no fear.

i.sp: all wanderers
i.ev: Tibetan འགྲོ་ཀུན; Sanskrit sarvasattvān. The glossary renders འགྲོ་བ as "beings" (locked in 1-24), and "wanderers" is not the term used elsewhere.
i.fx: all beings

atts.t:
For example, just as a magician conjures an emanation at a crossroads,
And cuts off the tens of millions of heads of a large crowd of people—
Whatever those to be killed are like, just so the bodhisattva
Fully knows all beings to be like emanations, and has no fear.

i.sp: conjures an emanation at a crossroads, / And cuts off the tens of millions of heads of a large crowd of people
i.ev: Tibetan "བཞི་མདོར་སྤྲུལ་བྱས་ཏེ། སྐྱེ་བོ་ཕལ་ཆེན་མགོ་མང་...གཅོད་" and Skt nirmiṇitvā...mahato janasya: the large crowd that is beheaded is itself the conjured emanation. bo-rangjung 1-18: "སྐྱེ་བོའི་ཚོགས་ཆེན་པོ་སྤྲུལ་པར་བྱས་ཏེ" (conjures a great crowd of people). The English singular "an emanation" and a separate "large crowd of people" lets the victims be read as real people, which blurs the point of the analogy ("those to be killed" are illusions).
i.fx: conjures a large crowd of people as emanations at a crossroads, / And cuts off the many millions of heads of that crowd

judge.reason: Both translations are highly accurate and clear; A's "wanderers" and B's "beings" are both acceptable and standard renderings of "'gro ba."

atts.t:
Whoever mounts it, going in any direction is not apprehended;
Though taught as going to nirvāṇa, no going is apprehended.
For example, just as a dead person has nowhere to go,
For this reason, it is fully proclaimed as "nirvāṇa."

i.sp: a dead person
i.ev: Tibetan text reads མི་ཤི, but Sanskrit has agni nirvṛta (fire extinguished), and Mipham (bo-mipham 1-21: བུད་ཤིང་ཟད་པས་མེ་ཤི་བ་ན་མེ་དེ་ཡིས་ཕྱོགས་གཞན་དུ་འགྲོ་རྒྱུ་མེད) and Khenrab (bo-khenrab 1-21) read the example as a fire that has gone out; only Rangjung reads a person. The English should flag this.
i.fx: a dead person [Mipham, Khenrab and the Sanskrit read: a fire that has gone out] has nowhere to go

i.sp: it is fully proclaimed as "nirvāṇa."
i.ev: The subject of རབ་ཏུ་བརྗོད་པ་ is གང་ཟག་དེ་ "that person" (bo-mipham 1-21: གང་ཟག་དེ་ནི་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་ཞེས་རབ་ཏུ་བརྗོད་པ; bo-rangjung 1-21), not an unspecified "it".
i.fx: that person is fully proclaimed as "nirvāṇa."

atts.t:
Whoever mounts it, going in any direction is not apprehended;
Though taught as going to nirvāṇa, no going is apprehended.
For example, just as a dead person [Mipham, Khenrab and the Sanskrit read: a fire that has gone out] has nowhere to go,
For this reason, that person is fully proclaimed as "nirvāṇa."

i.sp: [Mipham, Khenrab and the Sanskrit read: a fire that has gone out]
i.ev: The Tibetan root reads "དཔེར་ན་མི་ཤི་" (a dead person), which the English already renders. The bracketed variant-reading note is not in the Tibetan and sits inside the verse text (bo-mipham and bo-khenrab 1-21 read "མེ་ཤི"; bo-rangjung reads "མི་ཤི"); it is a philological note, not part of the translation.
i.fx: Remove the bracket from the verse line and move it to a note: "For example, just as a dead person has nowhere to go,"

judge.reason: B correctly identifies the referent of "de ni" as "that person" (the bodhisattva), matching the commentary, while A incorrectly uses "it."

atts.t:
The bodhisattva is not apprehended in the prior limit, the later limit,
Or the present; the three times are pure.
They are unconditioned and free from elaboration;
This is the practice of the supreme perfection of wisdom.

i.sp: They are unconditioned and free from elaboration
i.ev: Tibetan གང་དག་དེ་ནི་འདུས་མ་བྱས་ཡིན་སྤྲོས་མེད; Mipham (bo-mipham 1-22: གང་དག་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དེ་ནི་འདུས་མ་བྱས་ཡིན་པས་... སྤྲོས་པ་མེད) takes the subject to be the bodhisattva; Sanskrit yo śuddha so anabhisaṃskṛtu. Plural "They" can be read as the three times.
i.fx: That [bodhisattva] is unconditioned and free from elaboration

atts.t:
The bodhisattva is not apprehended in the prior limit, the later limit,
Or the present; the three times are pure.
That bodhisattva is unconditioned and free from elaboration;
This is the practice of the supreme perfection of wisdom.

judge.reason: B clarifies that "unconditioned" refers to "That bodhisattva," avoiding A's ambiguous "They," which could erroneously be read as referring to the three times.

atts.t:
Permanent and impermanent, happiness and suffering, pleasant and unpleasant,
Self and selflessness, suchness and likewise emptiness;
One does not abide in attaining the fruit, nor in the stage of an arhat,
And one does not abide in the stage of a pratyekabuddha, nor likewise the stage of a Buddha.

i.sp: Permanent and impermanent ... suchness and likewise emptiness;
i.ev: The first two lines are bare lists; in the Tibetan they are the objects of མི་གནས་ in line 3 (bo-mipham 2-2: རྟག་པ་དང་མི་རྟག་པ་... གང་ལའང་མི་གནས). The English leaves them syntactically unattached.
i.fx: One does not abide in the permanent and impermanent, happiness and suffering, pleasant and unpleasant, self and selflessness, suchness and likewise emptiness;

atts.t:
One does not abide in the permanent and impermanent, happiness and suffering, pleasant and unpleasant,
Self and selflessness, suchness and likewise emptiness;
One does not abide in attaining the fruit, nor in the stage of an arhat,
And one does not abide in the stage of a pratyekabuddha, nor likewise the stage of a Buddha.

judge.reason: B clarifies the syntax by inserting 'in the' in line 1, making it clear that the non-abiding applies to the entire list.

i.sp: Likewise, one does not abide in the conditioned
i.ev: Tibetan དེ་བཞིན་འདུས་བྱས་ལ་ཡང་མི་གནས་: the subject remains the Guide (འདྲེན་པ), whose mind abides in neither (bo-mipham 2-3: ཐུགས་ ... འདུས་བྱས་ཁམས་གསུམ་འཁོར་བའི་ཕྱོགས་ལ་ཡང་མི་གནས). "one" shifts the subject.
i.fx: Likewise, he does not abide in the conditioned either, but practices without abiding;

judge.reason: A correctly uses 'he' to maintain the subject as the Guide in the second line, whereas B switches to the generic 'one'.

atts.t:
Those who think they will become śrāvakas of the Sugata,
And those who wish to become pratyekabuddhas, and likewise Dharma Kings, Buddhas,
Cannot attain this without relying on this patience,
Just as one does not see a crossing to go from this shore to the other.

i.sp: Dharma Kings, Buddhas
i.ev: Tibetan ཆོས་རྒྱལ་ is a single term (Dharma King, i.e. Buddha: bo-mipham 2-4 ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་པོ་སངས་རྒྱས); the comma-separated "Buddhas" reads as an extra category. "Buddhas" is a gloss, not a separate word in the verse.
i.fx: Dharma Kings

atts.t:
Those who think, "May I become a śrāvaka of the Sugata,"
Or wish to become a pratyekabuddha, and likewise a Dharma King, a Buddha,
Cannot attain them without relying on this patience,
Just as one sees no crossing to go from this shore to the other.

judge.reason: B translates the intention slightly more naturally and correctly uses 'them' to refer to the multiple fruits/goals rather than 'this'.

atts.t:
The teaching of the Dharma, the listening, and whatever is taught,
The attainment of the fruit, the pratyekabuddha, and likewise the Protector of the World,
And whatever nirvāṇa is attained by the brilliance of the wise—
The Tathāgata has taught that all these are like an illusion.

i.sp: by the brilliance of the wise
i.ev: Tibetan མཁས་པ་གསལ་བས་ཐོབ་པ: མཁས་པ་ and གསལ་བ་ describe the agents (the wise and lucid); Mipham (bo-mipham 2-5: མཁས་པ་བློ་གསལ་བས་ཐོབ་པའི་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ), Sanskrit vidupaṇḍitehi "by the learned wise". "Brilliance" turns a quality of the persons into an instrument.
i.fx: by the wise and lucid

atts.t:
The teaching of the Dharma, the listening, and whatever is taught,
The attainment of the fruit, the pratyekabuddha, and likewise the Protector of the World,
And whatever nirvāṇa is attained by the wise and lucid—
The Tathāgata has taught that all these are like an illusion.

judge.reason: A accurately renders 'the wise and lucid' describing the person who attains, whereas B turns 'lucid' into an abstract noun 'brilliance'.

i.sp: Those who are free from perception, having attained this,
i.ev: Tibetan: གང་དག་འདུ་ཤེས་བྲལ་བ་འདི་ནི་རྗེས་ཐོབ་པ། — those who attain this freedom from perception (Sanskrit ye atra saṃjñavigamaṃ anuprāpnuvanti). Mipham 2-11: འདུ་ཤེས་ཐམས་ཅད་དང་བྲལ་བ ... འདི་ལྟ་བུ་ནི་གང་གིས་རྗེས་སུ་ཐོབ་པ་དེ་དག — freedom from perception is what is attained. The English makes "free from perception" a description of the people and leaves "this" without a clear referent.
i.fx: Those who attain this freedom from perception,

judge.reason: B's phrasing 'attain this freedom from perception' translates the Tibetan syntax much more naturally than A's disjointed construction.

atts.t:
This perfection of wisdom in which the Protectors practice—
Whoever pays respect, retains, and masters it,
Will not be harmed by poison, weapons, fire, or water,
And Māra and the factions of Māra will find no opportunity against them.

i.sp: masters it
i.ev: Tibetan: ཆུབ་བྱེད་པ. Mipham 2-14: དོན་ཡིད་ལ་ཆུད་པར་བྱེད་པ (grasps the meaning in mind); Khenrab 2-14: སྒོམ... ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱིས་དོན་ཀུན་ཆུབ་པར་བྱེད་པ (comprehends the meaning through the wisdom of hearing, reflection and meditation). The commentaries gloss it as understanding the meaning, not "mastering".
i.fx: fully understands its meaning

atts.t:
This perfection of wisdom in which the Protectors practice—
Whoever pays respect, retains, and fully understands its meaning,
Will not be harmed by poison, weapons, fire, or water,
And Māra and the factions of Māra will find no opportunity against them.

judge.reason: B translates 'chub byed pa' more concisely and naturally as 'masters it' rather than padding it to 'fully understands its meaning'.

atts.t:
If someone, of a Sugata who has passed into parinirvāṇa,
Were to build stūpas of the seven precious things and make offerings,
And with those stūpas of the Sugata, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
Were to fill thousands of millions of fields,

i.sp: If someone, of a Sugata who has passed into parinirvāṇa, / Were to build stūpas of the seven precious things
i.ev: Tibetan: བདེ་གཤེགས་ཡོངས་སུ་མྱ་ངན་འདས་པ་ཡི། མཆོད་རྟེན་རིན་ཆེན་བདུན་ལས་བྱས། — "of the Sugata" qualifies the stūpas (Mipham 2-15: རིང་སྲེལ་གྱི་སྙིང་པོ་ཅན་གྱི་མཆོད་རྟེན, a stūpa of the parinirvāṇa Sugata). In English the genitive phrase is stranded between "someone" and the verb, hard to parse.
i.fx: If someone were to build stūpas of the seven precious things for a Sugata who has passed into parinirvāṇa and make offerings,

atts.t:
If someone were to build stūpas of the seven precious things
For a Sugata who has passed into parinirvāṇa and make offerings,
And with those stūpas of the Sugata, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
Were to fill thousands of millions of fields,

judge.reason: B has a much smoother and more natural English word order by placing 'For a Sugata' after the verb phrase.

atts.t:
Fully conceiving of this, if in infinite millions of fields
All the sentient beings, however many reside there,
Doing no other work, with divine flowers, supreme incense, and
Ointments, were to make offerings for an eon or more in the three times—

i.sp: Fully conceiving of this, if
i.ev: Tibetan: ཡོངས་སུ་བརྟག་བཟུང་ ... ན. Mipham 2-15/16: ཡོངས་སུ་བརྟག་པ་བཟུང་བའི་དཔེར་བྱ་ན (taking it as an illustrative supposition); Khenrab 2-15: བརྟག་པ་མཐའ་བཟུང་གི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་དཔེར་བྱས་ན; Rangjung: ཡོངས་སུ་བརྟག་པའི་ཐབས་བཟུང་ན (if one adopts a way of assessing). The phrase introduces a hypothetical illustration, not an act of mentally "conceiving of this"; "of this" has no basis in the Tibetan.
i.fx: By way of supposition, if

i.sp: in the three times
i.ev: Tibetan: དུས་གསུམ་བསྐལ་པའམ་དེ་བས་ལྷག་མཆོད་ལ། Mipham 2-15: ཉིན་མཚན་རེ་རེ་ཞིང་དུས་གསུམ་དུ་མ་ཆག་པར ... བསྐལ་པའམ་དེ་བས་ཀྱང་ལྷག་པར་མཆོད་ན; Rangjung 2-15: དུས་སྔ་དྲོ་གུང་ཕྱི་དྲོ་གསུམ་དུ (morning, noon, afternoon). The "three times" are the three periods of each day, not past, present and future, which is how the bare English "the three times" reads.
i.fx: at the three times of each day, for an eon or more

atts.t:
By way of supposition, if in infinite millions of fields
All the sentient beings, however many reside there,
Doing no other work, with divine flowers, supreme incense, and
Ointments, were to make offerings at the three times of each day, for an eon or more—

judge.reason: A's 'By way of supposition' correctly captures the commentators' gloss of 'yongs su brtag bzung' as a hypothetical assumption.

atts.t:
If a bodhisattva, while lacking full understanding,
Fully demonstrates form, perception, feeling, volition, and consciousness
As impermanent, they act upon a fabrication;
The wise never destroy phenomena.

i.sp: they act upon a fabrication
i.ev: བཅོས་ལ་སྤྱོད་པ་ : Mipham 2-29 glosses it as engaging in a mere semblance, a counterfeit of the perfection of wisdom (ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའི་གཟུགས་བརྙན་ནམ་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་བཅོས་མ ... ལྟར་སྣང་ལ་སྤྱོད་པ); Rangjung 2-29: ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་བཅོས་མ་སྤྱོད་པ. Skt pratirūpikāya carate = practises a counterfeit. 'Act upon a fabrication' loses that the object is a counterfeit perfection of wisdom and 'act upon' does not render སྤྱོད་པ (practise/engage in).
i.fx: they practise a counterfeit (of the perfection of wisdom)

atts.t:
If a bodhisattva, while lacking full understanding,
Fully demonstrates form, perception, feeling, volition, and consciousness
As impermanent, they practise a counterfeit of the perfection of wisdom;
The wise never destroy phenomena.

judge.reason: B is more faithful to the root text, whereas A adds "of the perfection of wisdom" based on the commentary.

atts.t:
Where form is not, feeling is not, and perception is not apprehended,
Consciousness is not, and volition is not apprehended,
And all phenomena are fully known as unborn and empty—
This is the practice of the supreme perfection of wisdom.

i.sp: Where form is not, feeling is not
i.ev: གཟུགས་མིན་ཚོར་མིན་ parallels མི་དམིགས་ and is explained as non-apprehension / non-clinging, not as non-existence: Mipham 2-30 གཟུགས་སུ་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པ་མིན་པ ... ཚོར་བར་མིན་; Khenrab 2-30 གཟུགས་སུ་བདེན་པར་མེད་ན་མེད་པར་ཞེན་པ་མིན་པ (one does not cling even to its non-existence); Skt na rūpa ... upalabdhiḥ (nothing apprehended). The English 'form is not, feeling is not' asserts that form and feeling do not exist, a nihilist reading the commentaries explicitly exclude.
i.fx: Where one does not take anything as form or feeling, and perception is not apprehended

atts.t:
Where one does not take anything as form or feeling, and perception is not apprehended,
Nor is consciousness taken as such, and volition is not apprehended,
And all phenomena are fully known as unborn and empty—
This is the practice of the supreme perfection of wisdom.

judge.reason: A translates the terse Tibetan syntax much more faithfully without adding explanatory phrases like "one does not take anything as".

atts.t:
Why is that? Those supreme speakers, having trained in this,
Demonstrate here that all phenomena are emptiness.
Hearing this, śrāvakas swiftly reach liberation,
And one reaches the awakening of a pratyekabuddha and the awakening of a Buddha.

i.sp: And one reaches the awakening of a pratyekabuddha and the awakening of a Buddha
i.ev: Three different persons are meant: Mipham 2-32 and Khenrab 2-32 assign liberation to śrāvakas of dull faculties (དབང་རྟུལ), pratyekabuddha awakening to those of middling faculties (དབང་འབྲིང་), and Buddha awakening to those of sharp faculties (དབང་པོ་རྣོན་པོ). The English 'one reaches both' reads as a single person gaining both awakenings.
i.fx: pratyekabuddhas reach the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, and those of sharp faculties reach the awakening of a Buddha

atts.t:
Why is that? Those supreme speakers, having trained in this,
Demonstrate here that all phenomena are emptiness.
Hearing this, śrāvakas swiftly reach liberation,
Pratyekabuddhas reach the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, and those of sharp faculties reach the awakening of a Buddha.

i.sp: Pratyekabuddhas reach the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, and those of sharp faculties reach the awakening of a Buddha.
i.ev: Tibetan line 4 "རང་རྒྱལ་བྱང་ཆུབ་དང་ནི་སངས་རྒྱས་བྱང་ཆུབ་རེག" has no stated subject; it names two awakenings that are reached. Making "Pratyekabuddhas" the subject is circular (those who already are pratyekabuddhas reaching pratyekabuddha awakening). bo-mipham 2-32 and bo-khenrab 2-32 supply the subjects as beings of middling faculties ("དབང་པོ་འབྲིང") and of sharp faculties ("དབང་པོ་རྣོན་པོ").
i.fx: those of middling faculties reach the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, and those of sharp faculties reach the awakening of a Buddha.

judge.reason: B translates the text as written, whereas A inserts commentarial subjects ("Pratyekabuddhas" and "those of sharp faculties") not present in the Tibetan.

atts.t:
When the sun's disk radiates its web of light,
At that time sentient beings exert themselves in their work; likewise,
When the mind of awakening emerges in the world for the sake of the knowledge of the wise,
Through primordial wisdom sentient beings become endowed with qualities.

i.sp: for the sake of the knowledge of the wise
i.ev: མཁས་པ་ཤེས་ཕྱིར : the wise (མཁས་པ) are the agents who generate the mind of awakening in order to attain knowledge. Mipham 2-34: མཁས་པ་དག་གིས་...ཡེ་ཤེས་ཐོབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་འཇིག་རྟེན་དུ་...སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པ་བྱུང་ན; Khenrab 2-34: མཁས་པ་བདག་གིས་...ཡེ་ཤེས་ཐོབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་...བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་སེམས་...བསྐྱེད་པ་བྱུང་ན. The English turns the wise into possessors of the knowledge and drops that the wise generate the mind in order to know/attain omniscient wisdom.
i.fx: When the wise give rise in the world to the mind of awakening in order to know (to attain primordial wisdom)

atts.t:
When the sun's disk radiates its web of light,
At that time sentient beings exert themselves in their work; likewise,
When the wise give rise in the world to the mind of awakening in order to know,
Through primordial wisdom, sentient beings become endowed with qualities.

judge.reason: A correctly captures "the wise" as the logical agent and "in order to know" as the purpose, making better sense in English.

atts.t:
Whatever tens of millions of hundreds of billions of Buddhas of the past,
And those who resided in infinite many thousands of tens of millions of fields,
And whatever Protectors of the World have passed into nirvāṇa,
Who taught the jewel Dharma in order to exhaust suffering—

i.sp: those who resided
i.ev: གང་བཞུགས་ is present: Buddhas who currently abide in the fields. Mipham 2-39 says of these ད་ལྟར་འཚོ་ཞིང་གཞེས་ཏེ ... ཆོས་སྟོན་པ; Khenrab 2-39 ད་ལྟར་འཚོ་ཞིང་བཞེས་...བཞུགས་པ; Skt tiṣṭhanti. The past tense 'resided' merges them with the past Buddhas of line 1.
i.fx: those who abide (dwell)

i.sp: Who taught the jewel Dharma
i.ev: ཆོས་སྟོན་པ is present/habitual: Mipham 2-39 and Khenrab 2-39 have them presently living and teaching (ཆོས་ཀྱང་སྟོན་བཞིན་དུ་བཞུགས་པ); Skt deśanti. The past 'taught' removes this.
i.fx: who teach the jewel Dharma

atts.t:
Whatever tens of millions of hundreds of billions of Buddhas of the past,
And those who abide in infinitely many thousands of tens of millions of fields,
And whatever Protectors of the World have passed into nirvāṇa,
Who teach the jewel Dharma in order to exhaust suffering—

judge.reason: A correctly uses the present tense ("abide" and "teach"), supported by the Sanskrit and commentary for the Buddhas currently residing.

atts.t:
If, when dedicating, the perception of a mind arises,
And if there is the perception of awakening, or dedicating with the perception of sentient beings,
Because of these perceptions, dwelling in views, the mind is attached to the three;
Since there is apprehension, it does not amount to being dedicated.

i.sp: or dedicating with the perception of sentient beings
i.ev: The line lists the three objects of clinging as a conjunction (mind, awakening, sentient beings), which line 3 sums up as གསུམ 'the three': Mipham 2-42 ... བསྔོ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་སེམས་ ... བྱང་ཆུབ ... སེམས་ཅན་དུ་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་བྱུང་ན ... བསྔོ་བའི་འཁོར་གསུམ་ལ་ཆགས་པ; Khenrab 2-42 same. 'Or' makes alternatives and 'dedicating with the perception of' garbles it into a different construction.
i.fx: and if there is the perception of awakening and the perception of sentient beings (as the recipients of the dedication)

atts.t:
If, when dedicating, the perception of a mind arises,
And if there is the perception of awakening and the perception of sentient beings,
Because of these perceptions, dwelling in views, the mind is attached to the three;
Since there is apprehension, it does not amount to being dedicated.

i.ev: Line 2 has a second ཡོངས་བསྔོ (“བྱང་ཆུབ་འདུ་ཤེས་ཡོངས་བསྔོ་སེམས་ཅན་འདུ་ཤེས”); bo-mipham 2-42 glosses it as the perception attached to the object of dedication (“ཡོངས་སུ་བསྔོ་ཡུལ་གྱི་སེམས་ཅན་དུ་འདུ་ཤེས”) and awakening as the basis of dedication (“བསྔོ་བའི་གནས་བྱང་ཆུབ”). The English renders ཡོངས་བསྔོ only once, in line 1.
i.fx: And if there is the perception of awakening [as that to which one dedicates] and the perception of sentient beings [as those for whom one dedicates]

judge.reason: A avoids B's insertion of "or," which inaccurately breaks up the list of "the three" objects of attachment mentioned in the next line.

atts.t:
If one acts upon signs, that is not dedicating;
But if there are no signs, it is the dedication to awakening.
Just like eating excellent food that is mixed with poison,
The Victor has taught that the apprehension of virtuous qualities is also like that.

i.sp: If one acts upon signs
i.ev: མཚན་མར་བྱེད་ means to take (the three wheels) as a sign, to make signs of them: Mipham 2-44 ཆོས་གསུམ་པོ་དེ་ལ་མཚན་མར་རློམ་ཞིང་བསྔོ་བར་བྱེད་ན; Khenrab 2-44 མཚན་མར་འདུ་ཤེས་ཤིང་རློམ་སྟེ་བསྔོ་བར་བྱེད་ན. 'Acts upon signs' does not convey this.
i.fx: If one makes a sign of it (takes it as a sign)

atts.t:
If one makes a sign of it, that is not dedicating;
But if there are no signs, it is the dedication to awakening.
Just like eating excellent food that is mixed with poison,
The Victor has taught that the apprehension of virtuous qualities is also like that.

judge.reason: A's "makes a sign" is a more precise and literal translation of "mtshan mar byed" (nimittaṃ karoti).

atts.t:
Hundreds of billions of blind people without a guide,
Not even knowing the path, how could they enter the city?
Without wisdom, these five perfections are eyeless;
Being without a guide, they are unable to reach awakening.

i.sp: Hundreds of billions of blind people
i.ev: བྱི་བ་ཁྲག་ཁྲིག (བྱེ་བ་ཁྲག་ཁྲིག, Skt koṭiniyuta) is the same expression as in 2-39 and 2-40, where the translation renders བྱེ་བ་ཁྲག་ཁྲིག as 'tens of millions of hundreds of billions'. Here བྱེ་བ་ is not rendered, so the same number is given two different values.
i.fx: Tens of millions of hundreds of billions of blind people (rendered consistently with 2-39)

atts.t:
Tens of millions of hundreds of billions of blind people without a guide,
Not even knowing the path, how could they enter the city?
Without wisdom, these five perfections are eyeless;
Being without a guide, they are unable to reach awakening.

judge.reason: B accurately translates both numbers in the Tibetan ("bye ba" and "khrag khrig"), whereas A drops the first one.

atts.t:
When they are perfectly embraced by wisdom,
They then gain eyes and obtain this name.
For example, just as a completed painting that lacks eyes
Earns no payment as long as the eyes are not painted.

i.sp: They then gain eyes and obtain this name
i.ev: The verse has no stated subject; the referent is the five perfections (Mipham 2-48: སྦྱིན་སོགས་དགེ་ཆོས་གཞན་དེ་དག་...ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་འདི་ཡི་མིང་ཐོབ་; Rangjung 2-47: ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའི་མིང་ཡང་འཐོབ་བོ). 'They' and 'this name' are unresolved in the English.
i.fx: the other perfections then gain eyes and obtain the name 'perfection'

atts.t:
When they are perfectly embraced by wisdom,
The other perfections then gain eyes and obtain the name 'perfection'.
For example, just as a completed painting that lacks eyes
Earns no payment as long as the eyes are not painted.

judge.reason: B is more faithful to the source text's wording, avoiding A's insertion of "the other perfections" which is only found in the commentary.

atts.t:
If one thinks, "I shall practice the wisdom of the Victors,
And I shall liberate many billions of sentient beings touched by suffering,"
A bodhisattva of awakening who thoroughly conceptualizes the perception of sentient beings
Is not practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom.

i.sp: A bodhisattva of awakening
i.ev: The Tibetan has only "བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ" (locked: bodhisattva); "of awakening" splits the term and adds words that are not in the Tibetan (Sanskrit "bodhisattvo"; bo-mipham 2-50 "བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔ་དམིགས་པ་ཅན").
i.fx: A bodhisattva who thoroughly conceptualizes the perception of sentient beings

atts.t:
If one thinks, "I shall practice the wisdom of the Victors,
And liberate many billions of sentient beings touched by suffering,"
Such a bodhisattva seeking awakening conceptually constructs the perception of sentient beings;
This is not practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom.

i.sp: bodhisattva seeking awakening
i.ev: Tibetan has only བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ (locked: bodhisattva); “seeking awakening” is an added gloss (bo-mipham 2-50: “བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དམིགས་པ་ཅན”).
i.fx: Such a bodhisattva

i.sp: many billions of sentient beings
i.ev: Tibetan “ཁྲག་ཁྲིག་མང་” (many ཁྲག་ཁྲིག, niyuta; bo-mipham 2-50 “ཁྲག་ཁྲིག་མང་པོ”); the same number is rendered “hundreds of billions” elsewhere in this batch (2-39, 2-47), so “billions” understates and is inconsistent.
i.fx: many hundreds of billions of sentient beings

judge.reason: A correctly translates 'འདི་ནི་' (This is) in line 4, whereas B awkwardly turns line 3 into a subject clause for line 4.

atts.t:
The purity of form should be known as the purity of the fruit;
The purity of the fruit and form becomes the purity of omniscience.
The purity of omniscience, the purity of the fruit, and the purity of form
Are equivalent to the element of space, indivisible and inseparable.

i.sp: indivisible and inseparable
i.ev: Tibetan "དབྱེར་མེད་གཅད་དུ་མེད" has two distinct terms: དབྱེར་མེད (indivisible, locked) and གཅད་དུ་མེད (cannot be cut off or distinguished). bo-rangjung 2-54: "དབྱེར་མེད་ཅིང་བློས་ཀྱང་ཐ་དད་དུ་གཅད་དུ་མེད" (cannot be conceptually separated as different). "Inseparable" duplicates "indivisible" and loses the second term.
i.fx: indivisible and not to be cut apart (as different)

atts.t:
The purity of form should be known as the purity of the fruit;
The purity of the fruit and form becomes the purity of omniscience.
The purity of omniscience, the purity of the fruit, and the purity of form
Are equivalent to the element of space, indivisible and not to be cut apart.

judge.reason: A translates 'གཅད་དུ་མེད' cleanly as 'inseparable', which flows much better in English than B's clunky 'not to be cut apart'.

i.sp: yet do not attain liberation
i.ev: Tibetan "རྣམ་པར་གྲོལ་བའང་མིན" means they are not (one-sidedly) liberated; bo-mipham 3-1 and bo-rangjung 3-1 gloss it as not being liberated into the one-sided nirvāṇa of the śrāvakas ("ཉན་ཐོས་ལྟར་སྲིད་པ་ལས་རྣམ་པར་གྲོལ་བའི་མྱང་འདས་ཕྱོགས་གཅིག་པ"). The English can be read as bodhisattvas never attaining liberation.
i.fx: yet they are not liberated (as the śrāvakas are, into a one-sided nirvāṇa)

judge.reason: B translates 'མེད་ཀྱང་' more elegantly as 'Though free from', and 'do not attain liberation' is smoother.

atts.t:
When a person who has set out on a wilderness path of many yojanas
Sees cowherds and excellent forests at the boundary,
They think, "These are signs that a village or city is near,"
And they find relief, with no fear of robbers.

i.sp: Sees cowherds and excellent forests at the boundary
i.ev: Tibetan "གནག་རྫི་མཚམས་ཀྱི་ནགས་ཚལ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས" is one phrase: excellent forests at the cowherds' boundary (Skt gopāla-sīma-vana-sampad). bo-mipham 4-3: "གནག་རྫི་རྣམས་གནས་པ་དགོན་པ་དང་གྲོང་གིས་མཚམས་སུ་གྱུར་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ནགས་ཚལ" (forests at the boundary between wilderness and village where cowherds live). The English makes cowherds a separate thing seen.
i.fx: Sees the excellent forests at the cowherds' boundary

atts.t:
When a person who has set out on a wilderness path of many yojanas
Sees the excellent forests at the cowherds' boundary,
They think, "These are signs that a village or city is near,"
And they find relief, with no fear of robbers.

judge.reason: A accurately reflects the syntax of 'གནག་རྫི་མཚམས་' as 'cowherds' boundary', whereas B adds 'and' which separates the compound.

atts.t:
Likewise, when thoroughly seeking awakening, whoever comes to hear
This perfection of wisdom of the Victors
Attains relief and becomes fearless;
They are not on the stage of an arhat, nor the stage of a pratyekabuddha.

i.sp: They are not on the stage of an arhat, nor the stage of a pratyekabuddha.
i.ev: Skt "na ca tasya trāso nārhantabhūmi na pi pratyayabuddhabhūmī" and bo-mipham 4-3: "དགྲ་བཅོམ་པའི་ས་ལ་ལྷུང་བ་མ་ཡིན་རྐྱེན་རྟོགས་ཀྱི་ས་ལའང་ལྷུང་བ་མིན" (they do not fall to the stage of an arhat or pratyekabuddha); bo-rangjung 4-3 glosses it as the fear of falling to the śrāvaka/pratyekabuddha stage being absent. The English reads as a plain statement of present stage.
i.fx: They do not fall to the stage of an arhat, nor to the stage of a pratyekabuddha.

atts.t:
Likewise, when thoroughly seeking awakening, whoever gets to hear
This perfection of wisdom of the Victors,
Attains relief and becomes fearless;
They do not fall to the stage of an arhat, nor to the stage of a pratyekabuddha.

judge.reason: A is more faithful to the text ('མ་ཡིན' = 'are not'), whereas B adds 'fall to', which is imported from the commentary.

atts.t:
When a person traveling to see the water of the ocean
Sees trees, forests, and mountains, it is still far away;
But when they do not see these signs, they think, "The great ocean
Is near," and they have no doubt about it.

i.sp: Sees trees, forests, and mountains, it is still far away;
i.ev: Tibetan "གལ་ཏེ་ཤིང་དང་ནགས་ཚལ་རི་མཐོང་ད་དུང་རིང" has the traveller seeing trees etc. and (knowing) the ocean is still far; bo-mipham 4-5: "ད་དུང་རྒྱ་མཚོ་དང་རིང་བར་ཤེས་ཏེ". The English has no subject for the judgment, so the clause is hard to parse.
i.fx: Sees trees, forests, and mountains, they know it is still far away;

atts.t:
When a person traveling to see the water of the ocean
Sees trees, forests, and mountains, they know it is still far away;
But when they do not see these signs, they think, "The great ocean
Is near," and they have no doubt about it.

judge.reason: B is more faithful to the concise wording of the Tibetan, avoiding A's addition of 'they know' in the second line.

atts.t:
Likewise, those fully entered into supreme awakening
Should be known as hearing this perfection of wisdom of the Victors;
Even if they have not received a direct prophecy from the Guides,
"Before long, I will touch the awakening of a Buddha."

i.sp: the Guides
i.ev: Tibetan "རྣམ་པར་འདྲེན་པས" has no plural marker; Skt "nāyakena" is singular; bo-mipham 4-5 and bo-khenrab 4-6 have a single Guide (the Buddha) giving the prophecy. The locked rendering is "Guide".
i.fx: the Guide

i.sp: Even if they have not received a direct prophecy from the Guides, "Before long, I will touch the awakening of a Buddha."
i.ev: Tibetan "སངས་རྒྱས་བྱང་ཆུབ་རིང་པོར་མི་ཐོགས་བདག་རེག་འགྱུར" is the main clause of the concessive "མ་གྱུར་ཀྱང". bo-rangjung 4-5 and bo-khenrab 4-6 supply "སྙམ་དུ་ཤེས/བལྟའོ" (they think/know "I will touch..."). The English leaves a quotation with no governing verb, so it dangles after the "Even if" clause.
i.fx: Even if they have not received a direct prophecy from the Guide, they know: "Before long, I will touch the awakening of a Buddha."

atts.t:
Likewise, those fully entered into supreme awakening
Should be known as hearing this perfection of wisdom of the Victors;
Even if they have not received a direct prophecy from the Guide,
They know: "Before long, I will touch the awakening of a Buddha."

i.sp: those fully entered into supreme awakening
i.ev: བྱང་ཆུབ་དམ་པར་རབ་ཞུགས = those who have set out/engaged on the path to supreme awakening (bo-khenrab 4-6: “བྱང་ཆུབ་དམ་པར་རབ་ཏུ་ཞུགས་པ”, who gradually enter through hearing/reflecting/meditating). “Entered into awakening” can be read as having attained it, which the last line (they will touch awakening before long) excludes.
i.fx: those who have fully set out toward supreme awakening

judge.reason: A supplies 'They know:' before the quote, producing a grammatically complete and coherent English sentence, whereas B leaves a hanging quote.

atts.t:
When writing down this perfection of wisdom of the Victors,
Various different modes of eloquence will arise;
Yet if, without accomplishing the benefit of beings, they completely deteriorate
As swiftly as a flash of lightning, this is the work of Māra.

i.sp: Yet if, without accomplishing the benefit of beings, they completely deteriorate
i.ev: Tibetan has no conditional or adversative: "འགྲོ་བའི་དོན་མ་བྱས་པར་གློག་བཞིན་མྱུར་དུ་ཡང་། ཡོངས་སུ་ཉམས་པར་འགྱུར་བ་འདི་ནི་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས" states that the practitioners do fall away quickly, and this is the work of Māra. Mipham (bo-mipham 4-12): "སྦྱོར་བ་ལས་ཡོངས་སུ་ཉམས་པར་འགྱུར་བ་འདི་ནི་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་སུ་ཤེས་པར་བྱའོ"; the subject of falling away is the practitioner, not the eloquences. "Yet if ... they" leaves the referent unclear and makes the fall conditional.
i.fx: and without having accomplished the benefit of beings, they quickly fall away completely, like a flash of lightning; this is the work of Māra.

atts.t:
When writing down this perfection of wisdom of the Victors,
Various different modes of eloquence will arise;
And without having accomplished the benefit of beings, as swiftly as a flash of lightning,
They fall away completely; this is the work of Māra.

judge.reason: A translates the clauses accurately without adding a conditional "if" that is absent in both the Tibetan and the Sanskrit.

i.sp: With a mind accompanied by views
i.ev: ལྟ་དང་བཅས་པའི་སེམས here means a mind with longing to look at (external objects), not doctrinal "views". Mipham (bo-mipham 4-16): "ཕྱི་རོལ་ཡུལ་ལ་ལྟ་བར་འདོད་པ་དང་བཅས་པའི་སེམས"; Khenrab (bo-khenrab 4-16): "གཟུགས་དང་ཡུལ་གྱི་བཀོད་པ་སྣ་ཚོགས་ལ་ལྟ་བར་འདོད་པ་དང་བཅས་པའི་སེམས". Sanskrit "sāpekṣacitta" (mind with longing/expectation). "Views" suggests wrong views (a different doctrinal category).
i.fx: With a mind that longs to look at external objects (a mind full of longing)

judge.reason: B rightly clarifies "lta" (looking/regarding external objects), whereas A's literal "accompanied by views" misleadingly suggests philosophical tenets (dṛṣṭi).

atts.t:
At that time, this work of Māra will arise:
At that time, whoever agitates many monks,
So that they do not uphold this perfection of wisdom,
Many other various obstacles will also arise.

i.sp: whoever agitates many monks, So that they do not uphold this perfection of wisdom, Many other various obstacles will also arise
i.ev: གང་དག་གིས་ is instrumental ("by whom"); the agents are the evil Māras, and "བར་དུ་གཅོད་པ་རྣམ་མང་གཞན་ཡང་འབྱུང་བར་འགྱུར" is the main clause. Mipham (bo-mipham 4-18): "བདུད་སྡིག་ཏོ་ཅན་གང་དག ... དེ་དག་གིས་ནི་མདོ་འཛིན་པའི་དགེ་སློང་མང་པོའི་རྒྱུད་དཀྲུགས་ནས". The English "whoever agitates" has no main verb tied to it and reads as human agents; the sentence is hard to parse.
i.fx: those by whom many monks are agitated, so that they do not uphold this perfection of wisdom—many other various obstacles will also arise

atts.t:
At that time, this work of Māra will arise:
At that time, those by whom many monks are agitated,
So that they do not uphold this perfection of wisdom—
Many other various obstacles will also arise.

judge.reason: B resolves the awkward, disjointed phrasing of A ("those by whom... are agitated") into a smoother and grammatically cohesive active sentence.

atts.t:
The suchness of the world and the suchness of an arhat,
The suchness of a pratyekabuddha and the suchness of the children of the Victors,
Are one itself, devoid of entities, not other—they are suchness;
The Tathāgata knows the perfection of wisdom.

i.sp: The Tathāgata knows the perfection of wisdom.
i.ev: Sanskrit "prajñāya pāramita buddha tathāgatena" has the perfection of wisdom as the means: the suchness is known by the Tathāgata through the perfection of wisdom. Tibetan "ཤེས་རབ་ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་པ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་མཁྱེན" is unmarked, but the English fixes it as the object of knowing, which the Sanskrit does not support.
i.fx: By the perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows (this suchness).

i.sp: Are one itself
i.ev: "གཅིག་པ་ཉིད་" means they are one and the same (identity of the suchnesses); "one itself" is not idiomatic English.
i.fx: Are one and the same,

atts.t:
The suchness of the world and the suchness of an arhat,
The suchness of a pratyekabuddha and the suchness of the children of the Victors,
Are one and the same, devoid of entities, not other—they are suchness;
By the perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows this.

terms: suchness of the children of the Victors

judge.reason: B correctly identifies the perfection of wisdom as the object of the Tathāgata's knowledge, not the instrument, aligning with both Tibetan and Sanskrit grammar.

atts.t:
Relying on the perfection of wisdom as a pleasure grove,
This is the domain of the Guides with the ten powers;
Though they completely deliver sentient beings from suffering and the three lower realms,
They never have the perception of sentient beings.

i.sp: Relying on the perfection of wisdom as a pleasure grove, This is the domain of the Guides with the ten powers
i.ev: The participle "relying" modifies the Guides in the Tibetan/Sanskrit ("ཤེས་རབ་ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་པ་དགའ་ཚལ་ལ་རྟེན་པ། ... རྣམ་འདྲེན་རྣམས་ཀྱི་སྤྱོད་ཡུལ", Skt "prajñāya pāramita ramyavanāśritānām"); Mipham (bo-mipham 4-25): "དགའ་བའི་ཚལ་ལྟ་བུ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་གནས་པ་ ... རྣམ་འདྲེན་སངས་རྒྱས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་སྤྱོད་ཡུལ". In the English the participle dangles from "This".
i.fx: This is the domain of the Guides with the ten powers, who rely on the perfection of wisdom as a pleasure grove;

atts.t:
Relying on the perfection of wisdom as a pleasure grove,
The Guides with the ten powers have this as their domain;
Though they completely deliver sentient beings from suffering and the three lower realms,
They never have the perception of sentient beings.

judge.reason: B resolves the dangling modifier by properly making 'The Guides' the subject of the clause modified by 'Relying on...'.

atts.t:
Whoever has firm faith in the Sugatas and bodhisattvas,
And applies their intention to the supreme perfection of wisdom,
Having completely transcended the two stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
Will swiftly attain the unassailable awakening of the Victors.

i.sp: applies their intention to the supreme perfection of wisdom
i.ev: Tibetan "བསམ་སྦྱོར་བ" names two things, intention (བསམ་པ) and application (སྦྱོར་བ); bo-rangjung 4-32 glosses "བསམ་པ་དང་སྦྱོར་བ་ཡོད་པས་ཐབས་ཤེས་ཟུང་དུ་ཆུད་པ", and Sanskrit has "āśaya-saṃprayogo". The English renders only intention.
i.fx: has intention and application toward the supreme perfection of wisdom

atts.t:
Whoever has firm faith in the Sugatas and bodhisattvas,
And has intention and application toward the supreme perfection of wisdom,
Having completely transcended the two stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
Will swiftly attain the unassailable awakening of the Victors.

judge.reason: A accurately renders both components of "bsam sbyor" as "intention and application," matching the commentaries, whereas B collapses them.

atts.t:
If those qualities of skillful means are fully embraced by wisdom,
They will swiftly reach the supremely wondrous awakening of the Sugatas.

i.sp: They will swiftly reach
i.ev: In "དེ་དག་ཐབས་ཀྱི་ཡོན་ཏན་ཤེས་རབ་ཡོངས་ཟིན་ན། ... བྱང་ཆུབ་མྱུར་དུ་རེག" the one who reaches awakening is "དེ་དག", the bodhisattvas; bo-khenrab 4-35 says "ཐབས་ཀྱི་ཡོན་ཏན་དེ་དག་...ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱིས་ཡོངས་སུ་ཟིན་པར་འགྱུར་ན...བདེ་བར་གཤེགས་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་བྱང་ཆུབ་མྱུར་དུ་རེག་པ་སྟེ་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་རོ". The English lets "They" refer to the qualities.
i.fx: If their qualities of skillful means are fully embraced by wisdom, they (those bodhisattvas) will swiftly reach

atts.t:
If their qualities of skillful means are fully embraced by wisdom,
They will swiftly reach the supremely wondrous awakening of the Sugatas.

judge.reason: A correctly reads "de dag" as "their" modifying the noun phrase, which reflects standard Tibetan syntax better than B's "those qualities".

atts.t:
Likewise, even if a bodhisattva has much faith,
If they are bereft of wisdom, they will quickly fall to ruin.
If their faith is fully embraced by wisdom,
Having entirely transcended the two stages, they will attain supreme awakening.

i.sp: they will quickly fall to ruin
i.ev: Tibetan "མྱུར་དུ་མ་རུང་འགྱུར" means they quickly become unfit/unserviceable; bo-mipham 4-36 explains "མྱུར་དུ་མ་རུངས་པ་སྟེ་ལམ་དམན་པ་སོགས་སུ་ལྟུང་ནས་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་ལས་ཉམས་པ", i.e. falling to a lesser path and away from the Mahāyāna path, not destruction.
i.fx: they will quickly become unfit (falling away from the path)

atts.t:
Likewise, even if a bodhisattva has much faith,
If they are bereft of wisdom, they will quickly become unfit.
If their faith is fully embraced by wisdom,
Having entirely transcended the two stages, they will attain supreme awakening.

judge.reason: B translates "ma rung 'gyur" as "fall to ruin," which accurately captures the severity of the spiritual destruction (Sanskrit: vilaya).

atts.t:
Those who practice thus, who are oceans of goodness and moons among speakers,
Are the refuge, the defender, and the dwelling place of beings;
They are the support, the intellect, the island, and Guides seeking their welfare,
Illuminating lamps, and imperturbable speakers of the supreme Dharma.

i.sp: Illuminating lamps
i.ev: Tibetan "གསལ་བྱེད་སྒྲོན་མ" gives two epithets; bo-mipham 4-45 explains them separately ("གསལ་བྱེད་དུ་གྱུར་པ" through teaching person-selflessness; "ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྒྲོན་མ་ཆེན་པོ" through teaching phenomena-selflessness). The English fuses them into one.
i.fx: illuminators, lamps

atts.t:
Those who practice thus, who are oceans of goodness and moons among speakers,
Are the refuge, the defender, and the dwelling place of beings;
They are the support, the intellect, the island, and Guides seeking their welfare,
Illuminators, lamps, and imperturbable speakers of the supreme Dharma.

judge.reason: A correctly separates 'Illuminators' (གསལ་བྱེད་) and 'lamps' (སྒྲོན་མ་) as two distinct terms, following the Sanskrit and the commentary by Mipham.

atts.t:
This Dharma of the Guides is profound and difficult to see;
It is not realized by anyone, nor is it to be attained.
Therefore, the Compassionate Benefactor, having attained awakening,
Felt little inclination, thinking, "Who among the masses of sentient beings will understand?"

i.sp: nor is it to be attained
i.ev: Tibetan "ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་མེད་པ" states that there is no attaining; bo-mipham 4-48 "འབྲས་བུའི་དུས་ན་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་བའང་མེད་པ" and bo-khenrab "དོན་དམ་པར་ཐོབ་པ་མེད". The English "is to be attained" turns it into a normative or future sense.
i.fx: nor is there any attaining of it

atts.t:
This Dharma of the Guides is profound and difficult to see;
It is not realized by anyone, nor is there any attaining of it.
Therefore, the Compassionate Benefactor, having attained awakening,
Felt little inclination, thinking, "Who among the masses of sentient beings will understand?"

i.sp: Felt little inclination, thinking
i.ev: Tibetan "ཐུགས་ཁྲལ་ཆུང་བར་མཛད" (little concern/exertion); bo-mipham 4-48 states the object: "ཆོས་སྟོན་པ་ལ་ཐུགས་ཁྲལ་ཆུང་བར་མཛད" (little concern for teaching the Dharma); Sanskrit "alpotsuko". The English leaves open what he was disinclined toward.
i.fx: Felt little inclination to teach, thinking, "Who among the masses of sentient beings will understand?"

judge.reason: Both translations accurately capture the meaning of the Tibetan. The subtle difference in phrasing 'is it to be attained' versus 'is there any attaining' does not significantly change the meaning.

i.sp: Without the wisdom of the Guides
i.ev: Tibetan 'ཤེས་རབ་ཕ་འདྲེན་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་མེད་ན'. Mipham (bo-mipham 4-52) and Khenrab (bo-khenrab 4-52) both gloss 'འདྲེན་པ' as 'རྒྱལ་བའི་ཡུམ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕར་ཕྱིན' (the Victors' mother, the perfection of wisdom), i.e. the wisdom meant is the perfection of wisdom itself as mother of the Guides, not the Guides' own wisdom; the English 'wisdom of the Guides' invites the latter reading.
i.fx: Without this wisdom, the mother of the Guides, they will not attain it.

i.sp: Endowed with skillful means, must apply themselves to the perfection of wisdom; / Without this wisdom, the mother of the Guides, they will not attain it.
i.ev: The Tibetan given has three lines (ending "ཐབས་དང་ལྡན་པས་ཤེས་རབ་ཕ་འདྲེན་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་མེད་ན་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་མ་ཡིན"), with the words "ཕ[་རོལ་ཕྱིན་པ]" and "ཡུམ" not fully written; the English has four lines and supplies "perfection of wisdom" and "mother" from the Sanskrit pāda division and from bo-mipham 4-52 ("འདྲེན་པ་རྒྱལ་བའི་ཡུམ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕར་ཕྱིན") and bo-khenrab 4-52. Line count differs from the Tibetan, and the supplied words are not marked as supplied.
i.fx: Endowed with skillful means, one must apply oneself to the [perfection of] wisdom; without this wisdom, [the mother] of the Guides, it will not be attained.

judge.reason: A is more faithful to the root text. B adds 'the mother', which is an explanatory insertion drawn from the commentaries, not present in the root Tibetan or Sanskrit.

atts.t:
If a bird with a massive body of one hundred and fifty yojanas,
Whose wings are exhausted, lacks strength and skill,
And leaps from the abode of the Thirty-Three to this Jambudvīpa,
It will surely meet with ruin there.

i.sp: It will surely meet with ruin there.
i.ev: Tibetan 'ཉམ་ཉེས་གྱུར་པ་ཡིན'. Mipham (bo-mipham 4-53) and Khenrab (bo-khenrab 4-52) gloss it as 'ཉམས་ཉེས ... ལུས་རྨས་པ' (harm, injury to the body, wounding); 'ruin' overstates this and is not what the commentaries describe.
i.fx: it will suffer harm (injury) there.

atts.t:
If a bird with a massive body of one hundred and fifty yojanas,
Whose wings are exhausted, lacks strength and skill,
And leaps from the abode of the Thirty-Three to this Jambudvīpa,
It will suffer harm there.

judge.reason: B's 'surely meet with ruin' captures the severity of 'ཉམ་ཉེས་' (and Sanskrit 'vilayaṃ') better than A's milder 'suffer harm' for a bird plummeting from heaven.

atts.t:
They do not desire fame, and their minds are not entangled by anger.
Even if they become householders, they are always unattached to all things.
For the sake of livelihood, they do not seek resources by terrible means.
They do not practice mantras for fierce actions, nor mantras for union with women.

i.sp: nor mantras for union with women
i.ev: Tibetan 'བུད་མེད་སྦྱོར་སྔགས་མིན'. Mipham (bo-mipham 4-60) glosses 'བུད་མེད་དབང་དུ་བྱེད་པའམ་རང་དབང་དུ་སྦྱོར་བའི་སྔགས' and Khenrab (bo-khenrab 4-60) 'བུད་མེད་དབང་དུ་སྡུད་པའམ་རང་དབང་དུ་སྦྱོར་བའི་སྔགས': mantras to subjugate women or bring them under one's control (Skt strīprayoga-mantra), not mantras for sexual union.
i.fx: nor mantras for bringing women under one's control.

atts.t:
They do not desire fame, and their minds are not entangled by anger.
Even if they become householders, they are always unattached to all things.
For the sake of livelihood, they do not seek resources by terrible means.
They do not practice mantras for fierce actions, nor mantras for bringing women under one's control.

judge.reason: A accurately renders 'sbyor sngags' (prayoga-mantra) as 'mantras for bringing women under one's control', properly reflecting the commentarial explanation of magical subjugation.

atts.t:
They do not prophesy whether beings with the karma of desire will become male or female.
Utterly secluded in the perfection of wisdom, they are free from conflict and dispute, and their mind of loving-kindness is firm.
Desiring omniscience, they always possess a mind inclined toward the teachings.

i.sp: Utterly secluded in the perfection of wisdom
i.ev: Skt 'pravivikta prajñavarapāramitābhiyuktāḥ' (secluded, devoted to the perfection of wisdom). Mipham (bo-mipham 4-60) 'རབ་ཏུ་དབེན་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་མཆོག་ལ་བརྩོན་པ' and Rangjung (bo-rangjung 4-59) '...ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་མཆོག་ལ་བརྩོན་པ': they are secluded and strive at the perfection of wisdom; the English drops the striving and makes seclusion occur 'in' it.
i.fx: Utterly secluded, devoted to the perfection of wisdom,

atts.t:
They do not prophesy whether beings with the karma of desire will become male or female.
Utterly secluded, devoted to the perfection of wisdom, they are free from conflict and dispute, and their mind of loving-kindness is firm.
Desiring omniscience, they always possess a mind inclined toward the teachings.

judge.reason: B adds 'devoted to', which successfully captures the underlying Sanskrit 'abhiyuktāḥ' (brtson pa) that the Tibetan commentators confirm is the intended meaning for this clause.

atts.t:
For example, a man who engages in the phenomena of desire,
Having made an appointment with a woman, failing to meet her—
However many conceptual thoughts his mind engages in for a single day,
For that many eons, the bodhisattva will achieve attainment.

i.sp: For that many eons, the bodhisattva will achieve attainment.
i.ev: Tibetan 'དེ་སྙེད་བསྐལ་པར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར'. Mipham (bo-mipham 4-65) 'དེ་སྙེད་ཀྱི་བསྐལ་པར་བསགས་པའི་དགེ་བ་ཡང་...བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར', Rangjung (bo-rangjung 4-64) '...བསྐལ་པར...བསྒྲུབ་པའི་བསོད་ནམས་ཅི་ཡོད་པ་དེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར', Khenrab (bo-khenrab 4-65) likewise: what the bodhisattva obtains is the virtue/merit accumulated over that many eons. The English leaves the object of 'attain' out, so the comparison (a day of practice yields eons of merit) is lost.
i.fx: the bodhisattva will obtain the merit accumulated over that many eons.

atts.t:
For example, a man who engages in the phenomena of desire,
Having made an appointment with a woman, failing to meet her—
However many conceptual thoughts his mind engages in for a single day,
The bodhisattva will obtain the merit accumulated over that many eons.

judge.reason: A clarifies 'will obtain the merit accumulated' to accurately complete the Tibetan ellipse ('thob par 'gyur'), reflecting the commentaries' explanation of what is obtained.

atts.t:
Spoken by the Buddha, thoroughly practiced and clearly taught,
Knowing all these Dharmas to be nothing but mere expressions,
Even if one were to speak of them for many tens of billions of eons,
In the dharmadhātu, there is no exhaustion and no increase.

i.sp: thoroughly practiced
i.ev: Tibetan 'རབ་ཏུ་སྤྱོད་ཅིང་རབ་བསྟན་པའི་'; Skt 'prayukta prakāśita'. Mipham (bo-mipham 4-69) 'དེའི་དོན་རབ་ཏུ་རྒྱས་པར་སྦྱོར་ཞིང་བསྟན་པ' and Rangjung (bo-rangjung 4-69) 'རྒྱས་པར་...སྒྲུབ་བྱེད་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་རབ་ཏུ་བསྟན' show the Buddhas elaborating and setting forth the meaning at length, not the Dharmas being 'practiced' by someone.
i.fx: extensively set forth

i.sp: many tens of billions of eons
i.ev: Tibetan 'བསྐལ་པ་བྱེ་བ་ཁྲག་ཁྲིག་མང་བོར' is the identical phrase rendered in 4-54 as 'many tens of millions and hundreds of billions of eons'; the same number phrase should receive one rendering across the text.
i.fx: many tens of millions and hundreds of billions of eons

atts.t:
Spoken by the Buddha, extensively set forth and clearly taught,
Knowing all these Dharmas to be nothing but mere expressions,
Even if one were to speak of them for many tens of millions and hundreds of billions of eons,
In the dharmadhātu, there is no exhaustion and no increase.

judge.reason: B translates both numerical terms 'bye ba' (koṭi) and 'khrag khrig' (niyuta) explicitly, whereas A merges them. B also translates the first line more coherently.

atts.t:
Seeing the wilderness paths of the world, along with famine and disease,
They are without fear and then put on their armor;
Always striving until the final limit of the future and vividly knowing,
They do not generate even a speck of a weary mind.

i.sp: vividly knowing
i.ev: Tibetan རབ་ཤེས་ (Sanskrit prajānamāno) means knowing thoroughly/fully; Mipham 4-77 glosses it as knowing (all this) to lack inherent nature, Rangjung 4-77 as knowing it to be like an illusion. Nothing in the source corresponds to 'vividly'.
i.fx: fully understanding

atts.t:
Seeing the wilderness paths of the world, along with famine and disease,
They are without fear and then put on their armor;
Always striving until the final limit of the future and fully understanding,
They do not generate even a speck of a weary mind.

judge.reason: B's "fully understanding" is a more accurate rendering of "rab shes" (Sanskrit: prajānamāno) than A's "vividly knowing".

atts.t:
Likewise, at that time, the skilled bodhisattva also
Generates great compassion for all realms of sentient beings,
And having utterly passed beyond the four Māras and the two levels,
Abides in the supreme samādhi and does not touch awakening.

i.sp: the two levels
i.ev: Tibetan ས་གཉིས་ (Sanskrit dvaye bhūmim) is explained by Mipham 4-80 as ཉན་རང་གི་ས་གཉིས་ (the two levels of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) and by Rangjung 4-79 as ཉན་ཐོས་དང་རང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ས་གཉིས་; the bare 'two levels' could be read as any two bhūmis.
i.fx: the two levels of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas

atts.t:
Likewise, at that time, the skilled bodhisattva also
Generates great compassion for all realms of sentient beings,
And having utterly passed beyond the four Māras and the two levels of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas,
Abides in the supreme samādhi and does not touch awakening.

judge.reason: B is more faithful to the source text, which simply says "the two levels" without explicitly naming the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas as A does.

atts.t:
Whenever a skilled and brilliant bodhisattva
Practices this supreme samādhi of peaceful emptiness,
During that time they do not cultivate signs;
Dwelling in signlessness, they practice peace and profound peace.

i.sp: profound peace
i.ev: Tibetan ཞི་ལ་རབ་ཞི་སྤྱོད་: རབ་ is the intensifier 'utterly' (Mipham 4-84: རྣམ་རྟོག་རབ་ཏུ་ཞི་བ, utterly pacified), not 'profound' (ཟབ་མོ).
i.fx: practice peace, utter peace

atts.t:
Whenever a skilled and brilliant bodhisattva
Practices this supreme samādhi of peaceful emptiness,
During that time they do not cultivate signs;
Dwelling in signlessness, they practice peace, utter peace.

judge.reason: A's "peace, utter peace" better captures the poetic juxtaposition of the Tibetan "zhi la rab zhi" without adding an unwarranted conjunction.

atts.t:
Likewise, the brilliant bodhisattva is skilled in all
The knowledge and liberation of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
They do not dwell in them, nor do they dwell in the primordial wisdom of a Buddha,
And they do not dwell in the unconditioned, but know the nature of the path.

i.sp: know the nature of the path
i.ev: Tibetan "ལམ་གྱི་ཚུལ་ཤེས་ཡིན": ཚུལ་ is the manner/ways of the path; bo-mipham 4-95 glosses it as knowing "ཉན་རང་བྱང་སེམས་ཀྱི་ལམ་གསུམ་གྱི་ཚུལ" (the ways of the three paths), not the nature of the path.
i.fx: know the ways of the path

atts.t:
Likewise, the brilliant bodhisattva is skilled in all
The knowledge and liberation of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
They do not dwell in them, nor do they dwell in the primordial wisdom of a Buddha,
And they do not dwell in the unconditioned, but know the ways of the path.

judge.reason: B translates "tshul" accurately as "ways" (or methods/rules, corresponding to Skt. vidhi), whereas A's "nature" obscures this meaning.

atts.t:
If, when thoroughly questioned about their conduct and faculties,
A bodhisattva does not fully teach the dharmas of emptiness and signlessness,
And does not explain the dharmas of the irreversible stage,
They should be known as unprophesied.

i.sp: dharmas of emptiness and signlessness ... dharmas of the irreversible stage
i.ev: Locked term ཆོས → "Dharma"; in "སྟོང་པ་མཚན་མ་མེད་པའི་ཆོས" and "ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པའི་ས་ཡི་ཆོས" ཆོས is the teaching (bo-mipham 4-98: "ཆོས་ཟབ་མོ་ཡོངས་སུ་མི་སྟོན", does not teach / "འཆད" explain), so lowercase plural "dharmas" reads as phenomena.
i.fx: the Dharma of emptiness and signlessness ... the Dharma of the irreversible stage

atts.t:
If, when thoroughly questioned about their conduct and faculties,
A bodhisattva does not fully teach the Dharma of emptiness and signlessness,
And does not explain the Dharma of the irreversible stage,
They should be known as unprophesied.

i.sp: when thoroughly questioned about their conduct and faculties,
i.ev: Tibetan "སྤྱོད་པ་དང་ནི་དབང་པོ་ཡོངས་དྲིས་ལ" has an unstated questioner; the questions concern the conduct and faculties of the irreversible (bo-mipham 4-98: someone asks "བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ལ ... སྤྱོད་པ་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་ཡིན་པ་དང་ ... དབང་པོ ... ཡོངས་སུ་དྲིས་པ་ལ"; bo-rangjung 4-98: asked about the irreversible's conduct, faculties and signs). The English participle attaches to the bodhisattva ("a bodhisattva ... questioned about their conduct"), suggesting he is asked about his own conduct.
i.fx: If, when someone thoroughly asks about conduct and faculties, a bodhisattva does not fully teach the Dharma of emptiness and signlessness,

judge.reason: A follows the exact capitalization of the locked glossary term for "Dharma", which fits perfectly as the teaching of emptiness.

atts.t:
When Māra approaches on the basis of names,
He speaks thus: "These are the names of you and your parents,
And of your lineage back to your seven ancestors;
And when you become a Buddha, this will be your name."

i.sp: your lineage back to your seven ancestors
i.ev: Tibetan "བདུན་མེས་རྒྱུད་ཀྱི་བར"; bo-mipham 5-5: "མི་རབས་བདུན་གྱི་མེས་པོ་ཚུན་ཆད་ཀྱི་རྒྱུད་ཀྱི་བར" (the lineage up to the ancestor of seven generations); Sanskrit "anusaptam upaiti vaṃśo" (lineage to the seventh). Not seven separate ancestors.
i.fx: your lineage back to the seventh generation of ancestors

atts.t:
When Māra approaches on the basis of names,
He speaks thus: "These are the names of you and your parents,
And of your lineage back to the seventh generation of ancestors;
And when you become a Buddha, this will be your name."

judge.reason: A correctly translates "bdun mes rgyud" as the lineage going back to the seventh generation of ancestors, supported by Mipham's commentary.

atts.t:
Therefore, a wise one who seeks supreme awakening
And possesses strong intention, having definitely destroyed pride,
Just as a multitude of sick people rely on a doctor to be cured,
Should rely on a spiritual friend without wavering.

i.sp: without wavering
i.ev: གཡེལ་པ་མེད་པར is "without negligence/laxity" (Skt atandritena "without sloth"); bo-mipham 5-12 and bo-rangjung 5-12 gloss it as constant, unlapsing reliance (གཡེལ་བ་མེད་པར ... རྒྱུན་དུ་བསྟེན་པ), not lack of vacillation.
i.fx: without negligence

atts.t:
Therefore, a wise one who seeks supreme awakening
And possesses strong intention, having definitely destroyed pride,
Just as a multitude of sick people rely on a doctor to be cured,
Should rely on a spiritual friend without negligence.

judge.reason: A accurately translates "g.yel pa med par" as "without negligence", which is more precise than B's "without wavering" (mi g.yo ba).

atts.t: Just as the perfection of wisdom is empty of characteristics, Knowing the characteristics of all these phenomena to be similar to that, If one thoroughly knows phenomena to be empty and signless, Practising in that way is the wisdom practice of the Sugatas.

i.sp: Just as the perfection of wisdom is empty of characteristics
i.ev: ཤེས་རབ་ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་པ་མཚན་ཉིད་སྟོང་ is read in bo-mipham 5-15 and bo-khenrab 5-15 (citing the Eight Thousand) as "the characteristic of the perfection of wisdom is emptiness" (སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་མཚན་ཉིད་); Skt prajñāpāramitā śūnyatā lakṣaṇena = "has emptiness as its characteristic". bo-rangjung 5-15 allows "empty of characteristic" only as a second option, and the next line ("the characteristics of all phenomena ... similar to that") presupposes that emptiness is the characteristic.
i.fx: Just as the perfection of wisdom has emptiness as its characteristic,

i.sp: the whole translation (one line)
i.ev: The Tibetan is a four-line verse (four ། ། units), but the English is run together as a single line, so line breaks and the line-by-line correspondence are lost.
i.fx: Set the English in four lines matching the four Tibetan lines.

atts.t:
Just as the perfection of wisdom has emptiness as its characteristic,
Knowing the characteristics of all these phenomena to be similar to that,
If one thoroughly knows phenomena to be empty and signless,
Practising in that way is the wisdom practice of the Sugatas.

judge.reason: A correctly matches the Sanskrit and commentaries in translating "mtshan nyid stong" as "has emptiness as its characteristic", whereas B is missing line breaks.

atts.t: Completely famished sentient beings desire food, And those with minds attached to saṃsāra wander perpetually. Both self and the phenomena of self are unreal and empty, Yet the foolish themselves tie knots in the sky.

i.sp: Completely famished sentient beings desire food
i.ev: The commentaries do not read ལྟོགས་པ "famished" but ཡོངས་སུ་རྟོག་པ / ཡོངས་སུ་རྟོགས་པ "fully conceptualizing" (bo-mipham 5-16 ཡོངས་སུ་རྟོག་པ་ཅན་དུ་གྱུར་པའི་དབང་གིས ... ཟས་ལ་འདོད་པ་སྐྱེ་བར་བྱེད; bo-rangjung 5-16 and bo-khenrab 5-16 ཡོངས་སུ་རྟོགས་པས), matching Skt parikalpayamāna "imagining"; "food" is explained as the objects of desire (འདོད་ཡོན་གྱི་ཟས). The Tibetan as given may be a scribal variant; the English follows it against the commentarial reading.
i.fx: Sentient beings, fully conceptualizing, desire food (the objects of desire)

i.sp: the whole translation (one line)
i.ev: The Tibetan is a four-line verse (four ། ། units), but the English is run together as a single line, so line breaks and the line-by-line correspondence are lost.
i.fx: Set the English in four lines matching the four Tibetan lines.

atts.t:
Sentient beings, fully conceptualizing, desire food,
And those with minds attached to saṃsāra wander perpetually.
Both self and the phenomena of self are unreal and empty,
Yet the foolish themselves tie knots in the sky.

i.sp: Sentient beings, fully conceptualizing, desire food,
i.ev: The Tibetan as given reads "སེམས་ཅན་ཡོངས་སུ་ལྟོགས་པ་ཟས་ལ་འདོད་བྱེད" (ལྟོགས་པ = hungry, "utterly hungry"). The English follows the reading "ཡོངས་སུ་རྟོག་པ/རྟོགས་པ" (conceptualizing) found in bo-mipham 5-16, bo-rangjung 5-16, bo-khenrab 5-16 and Sanskrit "parikalpayamāna". The departure from the Tibetan wording is not flagged.
i.fx: Sentient beings, fully conceptualizing [Tib. text: "utterly hungry"], desire food,

judge.reason: A correctly follows the commentaries and Sanskrit (parikalpayamāna) by interpreting "ltogs pa" as a misspelling for "rtog(s) pa" (conceptualizing), whereas B translates the literal error.

atts.t: For example, just as poison is aroused by the perception of suspicion, Even if that poison has not entered inside, one will faint; Likewise, the foolish, asserting self and what belongs to self, Through the perception of that self, truly impermanent, are born and die.

i.sp: just as poison is aroused by the perception of suspicion
i.ev: དུག་བསླང་བ is "takes/swallows poison" (bo-rangjung 5-17 reads དུག་བླངས་པ; bo-mipham 5-17: "thinking 'the poison has gone inside'"; Skt viṣasaṃjñata abhyupaiti). The poison is not "aroused"; a person, on suspecting, believes they have taken poison.
i.fx: just as one who, through a suspicious perception, thinks they have taken poison

i.sp: Through the perception of that self, truly impermanent,
i.ev: The line says the perception of that self is unreal (ཡང་དག་མིན, Skt abhūto), not that the self is "truly impermanent": bo-mipham 5-17 བདག་ཅེས་བྱ་བའི་ཡུལ་དེར་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་ཡང་དག་པ་མིན་པའི་རྟོག་པ་འབྱུང་ཞིང་ ... སྐྱེ་ཞིང་འཆི; bo-khenrab 5-17 the same (བདེན་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་ཡང་དག་པ་མིན་པའི་ཀུན་རྟོག). Skt also has sadā "always": they are always born and die. The English wrongly predicates impermanence of the self.
i.fx: through the unreal perception of that self, are continually born and die

i.sp: the whole translation (one line)
i.ev: The Tibetan is a four-line verse (four ། ། units), but the English is run together as a single line, so line breaks and the line-by-line correspondence are lost.
i.fx: Set the English in four lines matching the four Tibetan lines.

atts.t:
For example, just as someone who, through a suspicious perception, thinks they have taken poison,
Even if that poison has not entered inside, they will faint;
Likewise, the foolish, asserting self and what belongs to self,
Through the unreal perception of that self, are continually born and die in impermanence.

terms: self and what belongs to self

judge.reason: A clearly captures the meaning of the poison metaphor as explained in the commentary (thinking one has taken poison), which B obscures.

atts.t: Just as there is grasping, so is complete affliction taught; Not apprehending self and what belongs to self is said to be complete purification; In this, without anything becoming an affliction or completely pure, The bodhisattva realizes the perfection of wisdom.

i.sp: without anything becoming an affliction or completely pure
i.ev: འདི་ལ་གང་ཡང་ཉོན་མོངས་རྣམ་དག་འགྱུར་མེད་པ means that in this (ultimate reality) no one/nothing becomes afflicted or purified (Skt na hy atra kaścid yo kliśyati śudhyate vā; bo-mipham 5-18 གང་ཟག་གང་ཡང་ཉོན་མོངས་པར་གྱུར་པ་དང་ ... རྣམ་པར་དག་པ་ཉིད་དུ་འགྱུར་བ་ཡང་མེད་པ). The English makes affliction itself the thing that something "becomes", obscuring that there is no one who is afflicted or purified.
i.fx: in this, there is nothing that becomes afflicted or purified,

i.sp: the whole translation (one line)
i.ev: The Tibetan is a four-line verse (four ། ། units), but the English is run together as a single line, so line breaks and the line-by-line correspondence are lost.
i.fx: Set the English in four lines matching the four Tibetan lines.

i.sp: In this, there is nothing that becomes afflicted or completely pure, / And the bodhisattva realizes the perfection of wisdom.
i.ev: Tibetan "འདི་ལ་གང་ཡང་ཉོན་མོངས་རྣམ་དག་འགྱུར་མེད་པར། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས ... རྟོགས" uses the adverbial "མེད་པར" (with/as there being none): the bodhisattva realizes the perfection of wisdom in the mode that nothing is afflicted or purified (bo-mipham 5-18: "...ཡང་མེད་པར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས ... རྗེས་སུ་རྟོགས་པར་གྱུར"). The English coordinating "And" loses this link.
i.fx: In this, there being nothing that becomes afflicted or completely pure, the bodhisattva realizes the perfection of wisdom.

terms: self and what belongs to self

judge.reason: B's "without anything becoming..." structurally aligns better with the Tibetan adverbial clause ending in "med par" than A's independent clause.

atts.t: However many sentient beings there are in Jambudvīpa without exception, If all of them were to generate the mind of supreme awakening, And practice generosity for many tens of millions of millennia, And dedicate it all as a cause for awakening for the benefit of beings,

i.sp: If all of them were to generate
i.ev: The verse closes with the concessive ཡང (བསྔོ་ཡང་ "even though ... they dedicate"; bo-rangjung 5-19 བསྔོ་ཡང༌, bo-mipham 5-19 "ཡང་ཡོད་མོད་ཀྱི"), setting this vast merit against the next verse, where a single day of practising the perfection of wisdom surpasses it. The English drops the concession ("If ...") and leaves the sentence without a main clause.
i.fx: even if all of them were to generate

i.sp: the whole translation (one line)
i.ev: The Tibetan is a four-line verse (four ། ། units), but the English is run together as a single line, so line breaks and the line-by-line correspondence are lost.
i.fx: Set the English in four lines matching the four Tibetan lines.

atts.t:
However many sentient beings there are in Jambudvīpa without exception,
Even if all of them were to generate the mind of supreme awakening,
And practise generosity for many tens of millions of millennia,
And dedicate it all as a cause for awakening for the benefit of beings,

terms: generate the mind of supreme awakening

judge.reason: B uses "Even if" which correctly captures the concessive meaning of "bsngo yang" (even if they dedicate) at the end of the stanza.

atts.t: Whoever diligently applies themselves to the supreme perfection of wisdom, And acts in accordance with it for even a single day, That aggregate of generosity cannot match a fraction of that merit; Therefore, one should always engage in wisdom without wavering.

i.sp: without wavering
i.ev: གཡེལ་མེད is "without negligence/distraction" (Skt atandritena); bo-rangjung 5-19 glosses it ལེ་ལོ་དང་བྱ་བ་གཞན་གྱིས་གཡེལ་བ་མེད་པར "without laziness or distraction by other activities".
i.fx: without negligence

i.sp: the whole translation (one line)
i.ev: The Tibetan is a four-line verse (four ། ། units), but the English is run together as a single line, so line breaks and the line-by-line correspondence are lost.
i.fx: Set the English in four lines matching the four Tibetan lines.

atts.t:
Whoever diligently applies themselves to the supreme perfection of wisdom,
And acts in accordance with it for even a single day,
That aggregate of generosity cannot match a fraction of that merit;
Therefore, one should always engage in wisdom without negligence.

judge.reason: Both "without wavering" and "without negligence" are valid and clear translations for "g.yel med".

atts.t:
When the sun, freed from clouds and arrayed in a lattice of light rays,
Rises, destroying all the dense, pitch-black darkness,
It eclipses all fireflies, living creatures, and spirits,
Along with the hosts of stars and all the light of the moon.

i.sp: all fireflies, living creatures, and spirits
i.ev: སྲོག་ཆགས་འབྱུང་པོ་ཐམས་ཅད is a single phrase "all living beings/creatures" (Skt prāṇabhūtām), whose faint light is eclipsed; bo-mipham 5-25 and bo-khenrab 5-25 treat it as creatures with a little light, not as a separate class of spirits. What is overpowered is their light.
i.fx: all fireflies and all living beings

atts.t:
When the sun, freed from clouds and arrayed in a lattice of light rays,
Rises, destroying all the dense, pitch-black darkness,
It eclipses all fireflies and all living beings,
Along with the hosts of stars and all the light of the moon.

i.sp: It eclipses all fireflies and all living beings
i.ev: The Tibetan "སྲིན་བུ་མེ་ཁྱེར་སྲོག་ཆགས་འབྱུང་པོ་ཐམས་ཅད་དང་། སྐར་མའི་ཚོགས་དང་ཟླ་བའི་འོད་ཀུན་ཟིལ་གྱིས་གནོན" has the sun overpower the light of fireflies and creatures, stars and moon ("འོད་ཀུན" scopes over the list). bo-rangjung 5-25: "སྲིན་བུ་མེ་ཁྱེར་དང་སྲོག་ཆགས་འབྱུང་པོ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་འོད་དང༌། ... ཟླ་བའི་འོད་ཀུན་ཀྱང་ཉི་མའི་འོད་ཀྱིས་ཟིལ་གྱིས་གནོན"; bo-khenrab 5-25 likewise speaks of the light of creatures with a little light. The English says the beings themselves are eclipsed.
i.fx: It eclipses the light of all fireflies and all (light-bearing) living creatures, along with the hosts of stars and all the light of the moon

judge.reason: B preserves the distinction between "srog chags" (living creatures) and "'byung po" (spirits), which A collapses into "living beings."

atts.t:
For example, a prince who desires the purpose of giving away wealth
Becomes the chief of all and is worthy to be approached.
If even as he is, he brings joy to many sentient beings,
What need is there to mention when he attains skillful means and is established in the kingdom!

i.sp: when he attains skillful means
i.ev: ཐབས་ཐོབ་གྱུར་ཏེ here means obtaining the means of ruling the kingdom (bo-mipham 5-27 རྒྱལ་ས་ལ་དབང་བའི་ཐབས་ཐོབ་པར་གྱུར་ཏེ; Skt paṭṭadhārī "wearing the royal diadem"), through consecration, in the prince parable; "skillful means" in the doctrinal sense does not fit.
i.fx: when he obtains the means (of rule) and is established in the kingdom

atts.t:
For example, a prince who desires the purpose of giving away wealth
Becomes the chief of all and is worthy to be approached.
If even as he is, he brings joy to many sentient beings,
What need is there to mention when he obtains skillful means and is established in the kingdom!

i.sp: desires the purpose of giving away wealth
i.ev: "ནོར་གཏོང་དོན་འདོད་པ": bo-mipham 5-27 explains that the prince gives away wealth to take care of his subjects and wishes ("དོན༷་འདོ༷ད་པ") to protect the realm for their benefit; the giving is the means to a beneficial aim, not itself the aim. The English reads as unclear.
i.fx: who desires to benefit others and gives away wealth to do so

i.sp: obtains skillful means
i.ev: "ཐབས་ཐོབ་གྱུར་ཏེ": bo-mipham 5-27 glosses it as "རྒྱལ་ས་ལ་དབང་བའི་ཐབས༷་ཐོབ༷་པར་གྱུར༷་ཏེ" (obtaining the means to rule the realm by consecration), and bo-khenrab 5-27 "རྒྱལ་སྲིད་ཀྱི་ཐབས་ཐོབ". In the simile ཐབས is the means of sovereignty, so the locked rendering 'skillful means' gives a misleading sense here (bo-rangjung applies skillful means only to the bodhisattva in the application).
i.fx: obtains the means of rule (consecration) and is established in the kingdom

judge.reason: The only difference is "attains" versus "obtains," which are equally correct in this context.

atts.t:
If any bodhisattva who has not obtained a prophecy
Becomes angry and initiates a dispute with one who has obtained a prophecy,
For however many moments of mind possessing the fault of hostility there are,
For that many eons they must don the armor from the beginning anew.

i.sp: possessing the fault of hostility
